summary: Source-anchored research for Collation-aware index key size. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: MongoDB warns that collation-aware index keys might be larger than keys without collation because it uses ICU collation keys; ICU describes these as preprocessed byte sequences that preserve the configured comparison order. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation.md ; https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/collation/architecture.html

For an indexed string comparison, the operation must use the same collation as the index; an operation with a different collation cannot use that index to support the string comparison. A larger collated index is therefore not automatically useful to queries using different string semantics. (high confidence)
For collated MongoDB string values, the index stores ICU binary comparison encodings rather than raw strings; comparing the encodings preserves the language-specific ordering. (high confidence)

Methodological inference: compare binary and collated versions of the same compound key pattern on representative text using the intended locale and strength, and measure the resulting index footprint and query behavior rather than applying a blanket expansion percentage. ICU documents that collation sort-key size varies with the alphabet and locale, and MongoDB's performance documentation lists inadequate or inappropriate indexing strategies as a source of performance limitations. (medium confidence) Sources: https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/collation/architecture.html ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/analyzing-mongodb-performance.md

Methodological inference: measure representative data under the intended locale and collation settings rather than applying a fixed expansion factor. ICU documents that sort key size varies with the alphabet and locale and is hard to bound exactly. Sources: https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/collation/architecture.html

ICU sort-key length depends on the alphabet and locale (via collation element size), and ICU compresses sort keys so that most regular character sequences produce compact keys. A source-string byte count alone therefore does not determine a universal key-size ratio. Sources: https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/collation/architecture.html

Comparison strength changes which distinctions matter: primary compares base letters, secondary adds accent differences and tertiary adds case differences. ICU encodes comparison levels in sort keys, so sizing should use the exact collation settings required by the application. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation.md ; https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/collation/architecture.html

Historical troubleshooting example: SERVER-60298 shows a Spanish-collation equality bound whose internal ICU bytes were exposed as invalid UTF-8 in explain output. Such transformed bounds should not be interpreted as the original string or used to infer its stored key length from the displayed characters. This describes the historical bug, not an assertion that current servers still emit invalid UTF-8. (low confidence)

ICU says maximum sort-key size depends on the alphabet and locale and that compression makes regular character sequences compact. Its bytes-per-code-point examples are approximate averages, not safe maximum bounds or MongoDB index-sizing formulas. (low confidence)

Collation strength selects comparison levels, and ICU sort keys encode level weights. Higher strengths or an added case level can change storage requirements; reducing strength also changes equality semantics, so size tuning must preserve required comparisons. (high confidence) Sources: https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/collation/architecture.html ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/collation.md

The PostgreSQL key-normalization draft explains that larger normalized keys can reduce B-tree fan-in, while compression and truncation can offset storage overhead. This is architectural context, not a description of MongoDB's index representation. (low confidence)
